rv.q: In Colette Robert’s quiet, mostly sure-handed production for Keen Company, “Crumbs From the Table of Joy” is a pleasure for several reasons: rarity, for one, this being the play’s first New York revival since its premiere in 1995.
What a joy it is to see an early work from a playwright you’ve long admired and discover something so terrific that you wish you could go back and see the play in its first incarnation.
There are more than crumbs to appreciate from this play’s table of joy, with its rich dialogue, heartfelt characters, socially conscious themes, period atmosphere, and quality acting.

Crumbs from the Table of Joy isn’t neat, has its lapses in logic, and rolls out any number of themes without entirely resolving them. But even early, lesser Lynn Nottage is stronger than a lot of what else is out there.

cn.t: Critics welcome this rare revival of Lynn Nottage's early 1950s memory play as a richly crafted, overlooked gem that showcases the Pulitzer winner's talent before her stratospheric rise.
